FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe biologics currently used to augment rotator cuff repair.
Discuss the normal rotator cuff insertional anatomy and the healing response after rotator
cuff repair.
Recognize the potential complications or adverse effects associated with biologics used during
rotator cuff repair augmentation.
Review the outcomes of rotator cuff repair with the use of different types of biologic
augmentation.
Overview
The goal of biologic augmentation is to re-create the native rotator cuff insertion site.

Successful biologic augmentation requires the following:
Proper combination of growth factors
Cells at the host site responsive to growth factor signal
Blood supply
Carrier or delivery methods that keep these factors at the correct location and release signals
at the appropriate time in the healing cascade

Overview
Several advances have been made in modulation of tendon-to-bone healing after rotator
cuff repair (RCR). The rotator cuff heals with fibrovascular scar tissue after repair, and
current research has focused on altering the scar tissue response at the enthesis, with
the goal of restoring and re-creating the native insertion. Surgeons must understand the
normal tendon-to-bone insertional anatomy and the healing cascade that occurs after
RCR.
Biologic augmentation has been hypothesized to potentially accelerate tissue healing
and recovery via mechanisms that increase angiogenesis, matrix synthesis and
remodeling, and cell recruitment, as well as alter inflammatory mediators and
metalloproteinases. Biologic augmentation is used to decrease the incidence of
mechanical repair failure. Mechanical repair failure is defined as any of the following:
construct failure (ie, anchor pullout, broken suture), failure of healing, or tendon re-tear.
In addition, biologic augmentation attempts to prevent additional muscle degeneration
with possible potential muscle regeneration.
Anatomy
Four zones of rotator cuff insertional anatomy (enthesis):
Tendon
Unmineralized fibrocartilage
Mineralized fibrocartilage
Bone

Tears predominantly occur at the transition zone at the tendon-to-bone junction (enthesis).

Anatomy
Normal insertional anatomy is not restored after RCR, and the enthesis is replaced by
disorganized scar tissue with impaired mechanical properties. A torn rotator cuff tendon
has low cellularity, poor blood supply of the enthesis, and degenerative changes.1
Injury Classification

Injury Classification
Massive rotator cuff tears are characterized by tear size greater than 5 cm or complete
detachment of two or more tendons.2,3 Repair of these tears often is technically
challenging, and predictable healing after RCR often is unsuccessful. This is because of
poor tissue quality, fatty infiltration of the rotator cuff muscles, muscle atrophy, and tear
pattern, which often is severely retracted and cannot be mobilized in a tension-free
manner back to the tuberosity (Resource 1).
RCR Healing
Fibrovascular scar tissue tendon to bone interface
Biomechanically inferior to native insertion
Healing Response After RCR
Inflammation (0 to 7 days): cytokine release4,5
Interleukin (IL) 1 beta
Tumor necrosis factor alpha
Nuclear factor kappa beta
Repair (5 to 25 days)

Remodeling (>21 days)
Transforming growth factor beta (TGF-ß): regulates and releases profibrotic factors from the
extracellular matrix (ECM)
Anti-inflammatory macrophages increase scar tissue formation consisting of type III collagen.
Anti-inflammatory macrophages express myogenic regulatory factors involved in the
development of mature myocytes.
Remodeling occurs, and type II collagen is replaced by type I collagen.
Timing of RCR Failure
Rotator cuff re-tears have been noted to occur within the first 3 to 6 months after repair.

Timing of RCR Failure
Several studies have examined the time to failure after RCR. Re-tear rates range from
17% to 41%, all of which occurred within the first 6 months after RCR. Miller et al6
performed a level III cohort study examining the outcomes of arthroscopic repair of large
(>3 cm) rotator cuff tears followed by serial ultrasonography at 2 days; 2 weeks; 6 weeks;
and 3, 6, 12, and 24 months after RCR. The authors reported a 41% rate of re-tears, all of
which occurred within 6 months of RCR. No re-tears were reported more than 6 months
after RCR. Iannotti et al7 followed patients who underwent repair for a rotator cuff tear
(tear sizes ranging from 1 to 4 cm) via postoperative MRI at 2, 6, 12, 16, 26, and 52 weeks
after RCR. The authors reported a 17% re-tear rate at a mean follow-up of 19.2 weeks
after RCR, with 68% of the re-tears occurring within the first 4 months after RCR.
Hernigou et al8 followed patients who underwent arthroscopic repair of rotator cuff
tears smaller than 3 cm via serial monthly ultrasonography and reported a 35.6% re-tear
rate within the first 2 to 6 months after RCR.
Biologic RCR Augmentation
Mechanical Augmentation
Scaffolds (Resource 2)

Allografts: from another individual, most commonly cadaver tissue
Xenografts: from another species
Porcine small intestine mucosa that is acellular and collagen based9
High rates of incomplete healing or failed healing
Poor postoperative functional outcomes
Not currently recommended for clinical use because of poor results and increased
incidence of wound complications
Porcine dermis (collagen repair patch)
Mixed results
Badhe et al10 demonstrated 80% healing rates, with high patient satisfaction rates and
improved range of motion, strength, and Constant assessment scores at a mean follow-
up of 4.5 years.
Sclamberg et al11 reported a 90% failure rate, with recurrent large tears observed on
MRIs 6 months after RCR augmentation.
The authors recommended against the use of this graft
Thon et al12 demonstrated 96% healing rates with the use of a bioinductive collagen
patch to augment large and massive RCR, 70% of which were revision procedures.
The authors concluded that use of bioinductive collagen scaffold is a safe and effective
option in patients undergoing repair of a large to massive rotator cuff tear.
Synthetic patch augmentation
Protects the repair site
Decreases friction in the subacromial space
All types used to reinforce RCR
Reports ranging from 78% to 96% repair integrity at final imaging follow-up evaluation13-15
Types of synthetic patches
Polypropylene patch
Poly-<small-caps>l</small-caps>-lactic acid bioabsorbable patch
Polytetrafluoroethylene patch
Bilayer absorbable poly-(4)-hydroxybutyrate scaffold
Dacron patch
Mersilene mesh
Outcomes


Outcomes
Mechanical augmentation (scaffolds) augments the rotator cuff tendon to increase tissue
thickness, increases the initial strength of the tissue at the repair site, protects the
repaired healing tissue, and allows for gradual tissue ingrowth. This type of
augmentation often is referred to as patch augmentation. Patches can be used to bridge
a gap if a rotator cuff tear is too large and cannot be mobilized back to the tuberosity
insertion, reinforce RCR by being placed on the bursal side of the repair in patients in
whom the tendon can be advanced only to the medial aspect of the tuberosity, and as
interposition tissue between the tendon and bone to aid in restoration of the native
rotator cuff insertion.13-18
Allograft tissues (acellular dermal matrices)/ECMs promote cell-to-cell interaction to
allow for growth factor expression, create an inflammatory response, infiltrate host cells,
and promote tendon-like remodeling if used to reinforce the RCR site. Grafts are
processed to remove donor cells, leaving behind ECM, which is composed mostly of type
I collagen; they function to strengthen the repair construct by increasing the thickness of
the tissue and optimizing the environment for host cells and growth factors to promote
tendon-to-bone healing. Wong et al17 evaluated the functional outcomes of 45 patients
with a massive rotator cuff tear who underwent arthroscopic RCR with the use of an
acellular human dermal matrix allograft augment. The authors reported improved
American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons, University of California–Los Angeles Shoulder
Rating Scale, and Western Ontario Rotator Cuff Index scores at a follow-up of 2 years,
concluding that the use of acellular human dermal matrix allograft was safe and effective
for augmentation; however, the authors did not report healing rates. Barber et al16
performed a level II prospective randomized multicenter trial examining the results of
single-row repair of rotator cuff tears larger than 3 cm that were augmented with the
use of acellular dermal matrix compared with RCR without augmentation. The authors
reported better Constant assessment and American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons
scores 2 years postoperatively and significantly (P < 0.01) better healing rates in the
augmentation group (85% intact) compared with the control group (40% intact), assessed
via postoperative gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance arthrography. No adverse
events were associated with the use of this graft material.

A recent systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrated the potential advantages of
various augmentation of RCR.19 This study highlights the heterogeneity of published
research (surgical indications, surgical technique, repair construct, measured outcomes,
assessment of healing) and the lack of a control group in most studies. No clear
advantage was noted with any of the repair constructs—allograft versus xenograft
versus synthetic grafts. The meta-analysis demonstrated a statistically significant
improvement in healing rates in augmented RCR versus standard RCR (62% versus 57%,
respectively) and select improvements in some patient-reported outcomes (American
Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons score; Figure 1).

Enhancement of Biologic Healing
Stimulate tendon-to-bone healing
Marrow venting (microfracture; crimson duvet)
Microfracture of the greater tuberosity allows for bone marrow elements, such as
mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), platelets, and growth factors, to increase at the repair site.
Marrow Venting (Microfracture; Crimson Duvet) Outcomes

Marrow Venting (Microfracture; Crimson Duvet) Outcomes
Although a large amount of basic science research has been performed on the biology of
tendon-to-bone healing, very few clinical studies have examined the results of local
marrow elements on RCR. In a level IV retrospective study with longer than 24-month
follow-up via MRI, Dierckman et al20 reported the results of repair for medium and large
rotator cuff tears (2 to 4 cm) augmented with the use of greater tuberosity bone marrow
vents. The authors reported a 91% healing rate and a mean overall Western Ontario
Rotator Cuff Index score of 95.7. This is a simple and inexpensive technique in which
perforations are created in the greater tuberosity to allow for extravasation of bone
marrow cells at the repair site.
Platelet-Rich Plasma
Autologous blood sample that has an increased platelet concentration compared with whole
blood21,22

Contains growth factors that can modulate the inflammatory pathway and theoretically
improve tendon healing
Increased platelet concentration by separating platelets from red and white blood cells
Varying amounts of platelets and white blood cells, depending on the preparation method;
however, an optimal ratio has not been established.
Differing platelet concentrations with variable growth factors released over time, which makes
the comparison of results difficult.
Bioactive red blood cells, fibrinogen, and leukocytes with different concentrations based on
method of preparation
Four categories based on leukocyte and fibrin content21:
Leukocyte-containing platelet-rich plasma (PRP): leukocyte count high, fibrin density low
Pure PRP: leukocyte count low, fibrin density low (autologous conditioned plasma)
Leukocyte-containing platelet-rich fibrin (PRF): leukocyte count high, fibrin density high
Pure PRF: leukocyte count low, fibrin density high
PRP is a mixture of growth factors: TGF-ß, fibroblast growth factor, platelet-derived growth
factor, leukocytes, monocytes, and macrophages.
Preparation Process21,22

Preparation Process
Autologous whole blood is obtained from a patient. Next, a one- or two-step
centrifugation process is performed, separating plasma from leukocytes and red blood
cells. This process results in concentrated platelets. Platelets are important because they
contain alpha granules, which contain numerous cytokines: TGF-β, basic fibroblast
growth factor, and platelet-derived growth factor. These cytokines promote tendon and
muscle growth and stimulate healing. Two main types of PRP exist based on white blood
cell concentration: leukocyte-rich and leukocyte-poor PRP. Leukocyte-poor PRP consists
only of the pure plasma layer, whereas leukocyte-rich PRP includes the buffy coat layer
that contains leukocytes.
Outcomes


Outcomes
Theoretically, the release of growth factors from the platelet alpha granules should
enhance cell proliferation of tenocytes and promote synthesis of ECM, chemotaxis, cell
differentiation, and angiogenesis, resulting in enhanced tendon-to-bone healing. PRP
can be delivered directly to the repair site, between the tendon and bone, or injected
intratendinously. Basic science data support that PRP inhibits the catabolic effects of IL-
1, IL-1 receptor antagonist, IL-6, IL-8, and matrix metalloproteinase-9 on tendon cells.22
To date, clinical studies fail to demonstrate substantial effects on tendon-to-bone
healing, re-tear rates, pain, or functional outcomes. No consistent, substantial benefits
have been demonstrated in postoperative functional outcomes or re-tear rates with the
use of PRP at the time of RCR.4,23-31 Zhao et al29 performed a level II meta-analysis and
Saltzman et al30 performed a level III meta-analysis, both of which examined the re-tear
rate and clinical outcomes of patients who underwent arthroscopic RCR with or without
PRP augmentation. Both studies reported no substantial differences in healing/re-tear
rate or patient-reported outcome measures. Hurley et al31 performed a level II meta-
analysis to assess the effectiveness of PRP or PRF in improving outcomes after
arthroscopic RCR. The authors reported that the PRP group for all rotator cuff tear sizes
had significantly lower rates of incomplete healing (P < 0.05) compared with the control
group (PRP group, 17.2%; control group, 30.5%). A subgroup analysis of medium to large
rotator cuff tears augmented via leukocyte-poor PRP resulted in significantly improved
healing rates (P < 0.05) compared with controls. Although the authors reported that PRP
resulted in statistically significantly (P < 0.05) better Constant assessment scores (PRP
group, 85.6; control group, 83.1) and 30-day (PRP group, 2.9; control group, 4.1) and
final-follow-up (PRP group, 1.2; control group, 1.4) visual analog scale (VAS) scores
compared with controls, these findings were not clinically substantial given established
minimal clinically important difference thresholds. The use of PRF resulted in no
difference in healing or patient-reported outcomes compared with controls. Rodeo et
al27 compared pure PRF–augmented RCR with standard RCR and reported no substantial
difference in healing rates at a follow-up of 12 months. In addition, platelet count had no
effect on healing, and regression analysis demonstrated that pure PRF had a negative
effect on healing (odds ratio, 5.8 for repair failure) at a follow-up of 12 weeks.

Growth Factors
Regulate matrix synthesis, cell migration, proliferation, differentiation, and inflammation
Found to accelerate healing with no change in the quality of the repair construct
Outcomes

Outcomes
To date, no human clinical trials have been performed to guide the use of growth factors
for augmentation of RCR. Rodeo et al1 examined the results of type I collagen scaffold
with osteoinductive growth factors TGF-ß1 through TGF-ß3, bone morphogenetic
proteins 2 through 7, and fibroblast growth factor at the tendon-bone repair site in a
sheep RCR model. The authors reported improved biomechanical properties 6 and 12
weeks after augmented RCR compared with RCR alone. No difference in maximum load
to failure was reported. Because of a lack of clinical trials and reliable methods of
application, the use of growth factors for biologic augmentation of RCR remains
experimental and mainly is used in animal models.
Stem Cells
Self-renewal, multilineage differentiation along various MSCs (osteoblasts, adipocytes, and
chondrocytes)
Current US regulations do not permit ex vivo culture expansion.
Autologous preparations of bone marrow, adipose tissue, and blood contain very few stem
cells according to formal International Society for Cell & Gene Therapy definition.
Limitations
Stem cells may change behavior after removal from the local host donor environment and
placement at the site.
The new site lacks appropriate signaling for differentiation to the cells of interest (ie, cells
need to be guided for appropriate differentiation).
Adipose-derived MSCs
Require culture expansion to isolate the desired population of stem cells
Not currently approved by the US FDA

Produce a stromal vascular fraction that includes fibroblasts, endothelial cells, mature
adipocytes, and adipose-derived stem cells
Placenta/embryo-derived stem cells
Pluripotent and can differentiate toward all three germ layers
No human studies have been performed; additional in vitro studies are necessary to
determine safety and efficacy potential.
Bone marrow aspirate concentrate
Bone marrow cells harvested that contains MSCs
Limited literature supports the clinical efficacy of bone marrow aspirate concentrate for the
augmentation of RCR
Autologous
Contains mesenchymal stromal cells and progenitor cells, which can facilitate healing
Three times more nucleated cells and more growth factors than PRP
Harvest sites: anterior-superior iliac crest, posterior-superior iliac crest, proximal humerus,
intercondylar notch, distal femur, proximal tibia, calcaneus
Does not require US FDA approval
Outcomes

Outcomes
Adipose-derived MSCs are colony-forming and adipogenic potential cells harvested from
fatty tissue, with a similar morphology to bone marrow–derived stem cells, and surface
marker protein expression, with higher colony-forming and adipogenic potential. To
date, no human clinical trials have shown that adipose-derived MSCs are a good option
for RCR augmentation to improve tendon to bone healing. Kim et al32 performed a level
III study comparing RCR augmented with the use of adipose-derived MSCs loaded in
fibrin glue and standard RCR. The authors reported that, although no difference was
observed in clinical outcomes at a follow-up of 2 years, a significantly (P < 0.001) lower
repair failure rate (14.3%) was reported in the MSC group compared with the control
group (28.5%). No substantial differences were found between the groups at final follow-
up with regard to range of motion, mean Constant assessment score, University of
California–Los Angeles Shoulder Rating Scale scores, and VAS pain scores.

Bone marrow aspirate concentrate contains a high concentration of growth factors,
including platelet-derived growth factor, TGF-ß, bone morphogenetic proteins 2 and 7
(anti-inflammatory and anabolic effects), and IL-1 receptor antagonist (decreased pain
response). These factors may promote tendon-to-bone healing; however, to date, no
clinical trials have shown the efficacy of this biologic augment in RCR.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Although an increasing amount of basic science data support the mechanisms and roles of
biologics, a paucity of high-quality clinical data is available on the safety and efficacy profiles of
these biologics and the effect of these biologics on structural healing and patient-reported
outcomes.
Mark as Complete
